nameStory: The Two-spotted Bumble Bee gets its name from the pair of bright yellow spots that shine like tiny beacons on its black abdomen. These distinctive spots make this bee one of the easier bumble bees to identify in the field. The scientific name 'bimaculatus' literally means 'two-spotted' in Latin, making this one of those cases where the common and scientific names tell the exact same story!
description: The Two-spotted Bumble Bee is a robust, fuzzy social bee that's about the size of your thumb. Like other bumble bees, it has a round, stocky body covered in dense, soft hair that helps it stay warm and collect pollen. The bee is primarily black with distinctive yellow markings, including its signature two yellow spots on the abdomen. These are important pollinators that live in colonies and can be seen visiting flowers throughout the warmer months.

idTips.label: Two Yellow Abdominal Spots
idTips.description: Look for two bright yellow spots on the black abdomen - they're usually quite obvious and positioned on the upper portion of the bee's rear section

idTips.label: Overall Color Pattern
idTips.description: Body is predominantly black with yellow markings on the thorax (middle section) and the characteristic spots on the abdomen

idTips.label: Size and Build
idTips.description: Medium to large bumble bee, roughly thumb-sized, with the typical bumble bee's round, robust, fuzzy appearance

idTips.label: Flight Sound
idTips.description: Makes the characteristic loud, low buzzing sound of bumble bees - you'll often hear them before you see them as they approach flowers

idTips.label: Fuzzy Texture
idTips.description: Covered in dense, plush hair that looks almost velvet-like and helps distinguish it from the smoother-bodied honey bees

habitat: Two-spotted Bumble Bees are found in a wide variety of open and semi-open habitats throughout New England, from suburban gardens and parks to meadows, fields, and forest edges. They particularly favor areas rich in flowering plants like gardens, prairies, and sunny clearings. You'll often spot them in backyards, along roadsides, and anywhere there's a good diversity of blooming flowers from spring through fall.

seasonality.spring: Queens emerge from winter hibernation and begin establishing new colonies. Look for large, solitary females visiting early flowers like crocuses and fruit tree blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with full colonies of workers foraging on a wide variety of flowers. This is the best time to observe and identify them as they're most abundant and active.
seasonality.fall: New queens and males are produced. Activity continues but begins to decline as flowers become scarce and colonies start to wind down for winter.
seasonality.winter: Only newly mated queens survive the winter in hibernation underground or in protected spots like compost piles. No bees are visible during this time.

funFact: Unlike many bumble bee species that are struggling with population declines, Two-spotted Bumble Bees are actually holding their own and remain abundant - they're like the success story of the bumble bee world, adapting well to human-modified landscapes and thriving in suburban gardens just as well as wild spaces!
confusionNotes: The two yellow spots are usually distinctive enough to separate this species from most other bumble bees, but some worn or faded individuals might be tricky. Memory trick: 'Two spots, two words' - if you see exactly two yellow spots on a black abdomen, you've likely found the Two-spotted Bumble Bee.
contextualKnowledge: In older field guides and scientific literature, you might see this bee referred to as 'Bremus bimaculatus' instead of 'Bombus bimaculatus' - Bremus was an old genus name that's now considered a synonym for Bombus. If you see Bremus in an old book, it's talking about the same bumble bees we call Bombus today.
compareHints: Among New England's many bumble bee species, the Two-spotted stands out for its clean black and yellow pattern with those diagnostic two spots. The Common Eastern Bumble Bee is similar in size but has more extensive yellow banding, while the Half-black Bumble Bee has a more distinctly two-toned appearance with less yellow overall. The Two-spotted's pattern is usually cleaner and more contrasting than its relatives, making those twin spots pop against the black background.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bumble bees, the Common Eastern Bumble Bee is distinguished by its predominantly black coloration with limited yellow banding, unlike the Brown-belted Bumble Bee which has brown fur, or the Tricolored Bumble Bee which sports distinctive white patches.
Among New England's bumble bees, the Brown-belted is most similar to the Red-belted Bumble Bee, but has a duller, more brownish belt versus bright rusty-red.
The orange band is what sets the Tricolored Bumble Bee apart from its many relatives in New England.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, the Perplexing Bumble Bee has more white hairs on the head and distinctive reddish mandible tips.
Unlike the Common Eastern Bumble Bee which has more irregular yellow patches, the Yellow-banded has clean, complete yellow bands.

Northern Amber Bumble Bees stand out from other New England bumble bees by their uniform golden-yellow body combined with contrasting pale head hairs—most other species have distinct color bands or patterns.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, Half-black Bumble Bees are noticeably smaller and have more defined black banding rather than the Common Eastern's more blended yellow and black pattern.

Among New England's bumble bees, the Golden Northern stands out for its uniform golden-yellow coloration, while most relatives like the Common Eastern Bumble Bee have distinct black and white/yellow banding patterns.
Unlike social bumble bees in its genus, the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee lacks pollen baskets (specialized hairs for carrying pollen) since it doesn't need to provision its own nest.
Unlike other cuckoo bumble bees in New England like the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee, the Yellowish Cuckoo has more muted, golden-yellow tones rather than bright lemon-yellow.
Red-belted bumble bees are much smaller than common eastern bumble bees and lack the solid yellow thorax of many other species.
